thread.title: Food Date Labels: What They Mean and How to Use Them
thread.title_full: Food Date Labels: What They Mean and How to Use Them

author: OLGA R. RODRIGUEZ - Associated Press
title: Food Date Labels: What They Mean and How to Use Them
text:
• More than 50 different date labels are used in the US.
• In the US, more than 80% of consumers discard food approaching the package date label at least occasionally.
• Date labels guarantee quality up until a certain point, not safety.
• Food date labels vary state by state and are determined by the food manufacturer.
• Over 50 different date labels are used across the US.
• Date labels are based on when the manufacturer thinks the product will taste its best.
• Unopened canned food can last for years after the date stamped on its label.
• Dry goods like cookies, crackers, and cereal have a long shelf life.
• People can use their best judgment by smelling and tasting the product for dry goods.
• Extra precautions should be taken with beef, chicken, or fish.
• The FoodKeeper website and app provide guidance on how long foods stay fresh and safe to eat.
• California is the first state to standardize food labels by banning "sell by" dates.
• California requires manufacturers to use two standardized labels: "Best If Used By" for peak quality and "Use By" for product safety.
• New York state lawmakers have passed a similar measure awaiting Gov. Kathy Hochul's signature.
• Infant formula is the only product required by the federal government to have an expiration date.
• Infant formula should not be consumed past its expiration date due to declining nutrients.
• People should use their own judgment and look for signs like mold, strange odors, and unusual colors to decide whether or not to toss out food.
• Follow your taste buds and practice food stock rotation to avoid eating poor quality food.
summary: With no federal regulations requiring standardized labels for dates on food except for baby formula, it’s no surprise that deciphering terms like “Best Before,” “Best By,” “Best If Used By,” “Enjoy By,” and “Sell By” can be mind-boggling. Dry goods, like cookies, crackers and cereal, also have a long shelf life because the low moisture in them doesn’t allow bacteria to grow.
